name: Chloe Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to any of it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a shuttle car in an underground potash mine, which is the salt they make fertiliser from. The cutting machine chews the face, and I take the load from it back to the belt, back and forth all shift, maybe a hundred trips. My dad worked in this same mine for thirty years, and some of the old hands still call me Ben's girl. I'm only two years in and I still clip the rib, the wall of the tunnel, now and then, and I hear about it at crib.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about life outside the mine.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm single and I live in a small house on the same street as my parents. My grandmother left me some money, and with my pay I've paid off most of the house, plus I've got about ten months saved. On Sundays I sing in the church choir and have lunch with the family. There are two other potash mines nearby, so jobs aren't scarce, but this mine is the one my family knows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's how I'd want it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm glad, and that the people selling all that AI stuff should be humbled a bit. At church people would nod. I'm not online much at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep going and finish learning my job properly. My dad will keep giving me tips on Sundays. The mine's been steady for fifty years and I'd expect another fifty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, keep paying down the last of the house, keep saving. Maybe I'd go for the cutting machine ticket in a couple of years, because that's what my dad drove. Nothing else would change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like things are as they should be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything already on your mind, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Potash prices are fine right now. The roof falls worry me more than anything. My dad had a mate hurt in one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the mine mean to your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything. My dad gave thirty years to this potash mine, and I'd like to give it thirty of mine.

say: I'd say I'm **glad**, and the AI sellers deserve to be **humbled**.
People at **church** would nod along, and I'd stay offline.
think: She keeps going and **finishes learning** the shuttle car job properly.
The potash mine has been **steady for fifty years**, and she expects more.
do: Pay off the **last of the house** loan.
Keep **saving** each pay as she does now.
Go for the **cutting machine ticket** her dad held, in a couple of years.
feel: **Calm**, as if things are as they should be.
S0.quote: My dad gave thirty years to this potash mine, and I'd like to give it thirty of mine.
fieldNote: Her sense of security comes from **family history** at the mine.
Her real worry is **roof falls**, a safety risk, not AI.
She'd follow her **father's path** to the cutting machine.

steps.text: Pay off the last of the house loan
Keep driving the shuttle car on the same crew
Go for the cutting machine ticket in two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't like the sound of that. Underground isn't the place for gadgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work that it's change for the sake of change, and that the company should look after its own people first. At church I'd say we'll get through it as a community. I wouldn't post anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd worry the shuttle car is an easy one to automate, because it's the same path every time. But robots spread slowly in this picture, so maybe I have a few years. The planning office would change first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and keep working. I'd keep saving and not take on anything new. If the company offered training, I'd only take it if my dad thought it was worth it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd rather not think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say do your job well and the mine will look after you. He's always said that. My dad always says that if you do your job well, the mine looks after you, and I'm not sure that's true anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider another mine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My family's here, and the other mines would have the same machines.

steps.text: Keep driving the shuttle car and avoid new commitments

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. That's too much, too fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong for big companies to throw out workers like that, and the government should slow it down. At church we'd pray about it, and I'd mean it. I'd vote for whoever promised to protect mining jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think my shuttle car job goes by 2031. I'm junior and I'm slow with anything new. A shuttle car underground runs the same route a hundred times a shift, and a robot would learn that route by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut spending right away and finish paying off the house so I have no debt at all. I'd stay close to my parents and help them out. I'd look at whether my dad's friends know of any work that needs real people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd be lying awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in those three years before robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working every shift I can, save everything. I'm not good at learning new things, so I'd stick with what I know until it's gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you lean on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My family and the church. That's what they're for. I wouldn't want government handouts unless I really had to.

I'd vote for whoever promises to **protect mining jobs**.
think: Her **shuttle car job** goes by 2031, as a robot learns the route.
As the **junior** who is slow with new things, she'd go first.
do: Cut **spending** right away and clear the house loan.
Stay **close to her parents** and help them out.
Ask her dad's friends about **work needing real people**.
S2.quote: A shuttle car underground runs the same route a hundred times a shift, and a robot would learn that route by 2031.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose the job** and sees no new skill path.
She'd lean on **family and church** before government help.
Her **paid-off house** is her main safety.

steps.text: Cut spending and pay off the house loan completely

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years and then robots around 2034. Still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the company should keep loyal workers and train them on the new machines. I'd say that at work and at church. I'd vote the same way as before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think I have about eight years in the shuttle car. That's enough to get the cutting machine ticket, but that might go too. Eight more years in the potash mine would feel like a gift, even if the robots come for the shuttle cars after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder and finish the house. I'd get the cutting machine ticket in a few years. I'd talk to my dad about what else the mine needs people for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd have time to think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a different job outside mining?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if I had to. Maybe at my uncle's hardware shop. He's said there's always a place for family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you change if you had more time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much. I'd keep going and hope the mine keeps us. That's the honest answer.

I'd say that at work and at **church**, and vote the same way.

The **cutting machine** ticket she wants might not last either.
do: **Save harder** and finish paying the house.

S3.quote: Eight more years in the potash mine would feel like a gift, even if the robots come for the shuttle cars after that.
fieldNote: Eight years feels like a **gift**, yet she still expects to lose the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. I'd be nearly 40.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time for the company and the government to do the right thing by miners. At church we'd say the same. I'd stay out of politics mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd keep my job most of that time, but I'd still lose it in the end. Ten years means I'd be nearly 40 before a robot drove my shuttle car, which is still young to start over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working and saving. Get the cutting machine ticket. Maybe in a few years ask my uncle about the hardware shop as a backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about family plans differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. If I married, I'd want my husband in a job that isn't going anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the hardest part of this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Knowing it's coming and still not wanting to change. That's me, though.

do: Keep **working and saving** in the potash mine.
Ask her uncle about the **hardware shop** as a backup in a few years.
S4.quote: Ten years means I'd be nearly 40 before a robot drove my shuttle car, which is still young to start over.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose the job** eventually, but not for over a decade.
She **knows** she resists change and says so plainly.
Family plans would favour a partner with a **steady job**.

steps.text: Keep working and saving at the potash mine

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'm slow to change and I'd be out with no plan. What would help is the company training loyal workers and keeping them on, not cheap payouts. I'd rather the potash mine kept me on and taught me something new than handed me a cheque and a handshake.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about family. For me it's the most important thing. Whatever happens, I'd want to stay near my parents and my church.

headlineQuote: I'd rather the potash mine kept me on and taught me something new than handed me a cheque and a handshake.
portrait: Chloe is a **27-year-old** shuttle car driver in an underground potash mine, still learning.
She's single, lives near her parents and has **ten months saved** and a nearly paid-off house.
She follows her **father's path** in the mine and avoids new technology.
She leans on **family and church** rather than government support.
She's **calm** in the plateau but **alarmed** when AGI comes by 2028.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd be out quickly with no plan.
whatWouldHelp: The company **training** loyal workers and keeping them on, rather than **cheap payouts**.
